title: Defender for Endpoint: Onboarding and Attack Surface Reduction
summary: Here you connect endpoints to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) and turn on its proactive hardening controls. You will establish the Intune-to-MDE connector, onboard Windows devices through an Intune EDR policy, and confirm devices appear in the Microsoft Defender portal. You will then roll out Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules using a disciplined audit-then-block strategy, naming real rules such as block credential stealing from LSASS and block Office child processes. Finally you will enable controlled folder access, network protection, tamper protection, and read your exposure score from Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management.
objectives: Describe MDE's cloud-plus-sensor architecture and the role of the Intune connector.
Onboard Windows devices to MDE through an Intune endpoint detection and response (EDR) policy.
Deploy Attack Surface Reduction rules and run an audit-then-block rollout to avoid breaking business apps.
Identify several real ASR rules by name and GUID and explain what each blocks.
Enable controlled folder access, network protection, and tamper protection.
Interpret the exposure score and security recommendations in Defender Vulnerability Management.

quiz.q: What does the Intune connector to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint primarily enable?
options: It installs antivirus signatures
It establishes trust so MDE can share device risk with Intune and Intune can onboard/deploy EDR policy
It replaces Conditional Access
It encrypts the disk
quiz.why: The connector creates the service-to-service trust that lets Intune onboard devices to MDE and lets MDE report each device's risk level back to Intune for compliance evaluation.

quiz.q: Why deploy ASR rules in audit mode before block mode?
options: Audit mode is required by licensing
Audit mode logs what would be blocked so you can find false positives before enforcing
Block mode does not generate any telemetry
Audit mode is faster to deploy
quiz.why: Audit mode records the events a rule would have blocked without actually blocking them, letting you discover legitimate business apps that would break and add exclusions before flipping to block.

quiz.q: Which ASR rule specifically protects against credential theft tooling like Mimikatz reading the LSASS process?
options: Block executable content from email client and webmail
Block credential stealing from the Windows local security authority subsystem (lsass.exe)
Block Office applications from creating child processes
Use advanced protection against ransomware
quiz.why: The 'Block credential stealing from lsass.exe' rule (GUID 9e6c4e1f-7d60-472f-ba1a-a39ef669e4b2) stops tools from dumping credentials out of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service.

quiz.q: What does Controlled Folder Access protect against?
options: Phishing emails
Ransomware modifying files in protected folders by only allowing trusted apps to write
Weak passwords
Outdated firmware
quiz.why: Controlled Folder Access guards designated folders so only trusted/allowed applications can modify their contents, blocking ransomware-style mass file encryption.

quiz.q: Tamper protection in MDE primarily prevents what?
options: Users running Office macros
Malware or local admins from disabling Defender features such as real-time protection
Devices from enrolling in Intune
BitLocker from being enabled
quiz.why: Tamper protection locks critical Defender settings (real-time protection, cloud-delivered protection, security intelligence updates) so they cannot be turned off by malware, scripts, or even local administrators.

quiz.q: In 2-4 sentences, outline a safe production rollout plan for a new ASR rule across a 5,000-device fleet.
quiz.answer: Start by deploying the rule in audit mode to a small pilot ring and review the ASR audit events and the attack surface reduction report for legitimate apps that would be blocked. Add per-path or per-publisher exclusions for confirmed false positives, then expand audit to the full fleet for a week or two. Once telemetry is clean, flip the rule to block for the pilot ring, validate, and progressively roll block mode out ring by ring while monitoring the Action center and user reports.

resources.label: Onboard Windows devices to Defender for Endpoint using Intune
Protect security settings with tamper protection

body_markdown:
## MDE architecture in one picture

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is a cloud service plus a sensor that is already built into Windows. The endpoint sensor streams behavioral telemetry to the **Microsoft Defender portal** (security.microsoft.com), where detections, the device inventory, vulnerability data, and automated investigation all live. There is no separate agent to install on modern Windows — you simply **onboard** the device (register its sensor with your tenant) and configure the antivirus/EDR engine. Onboarding plus the Intune connector is what makes a device both *protected* and *governable*.

## The Intune <-> MDE connector

First wire the two services together. In the **Microsoft Defender portal**: *Settings > Endpoints > Advanced features* and turn on **Microsoft Intune connection**. Then in the **Intune admin center**: *Endpoint security > Microsoft Defender for Endpoint* and confirm the connection status is *Available* with *Connect Windows devices...* set to **On**. This service-to-service trust does two jobs: it lets Intune onboard devices, and — crucially for Lesson 3 — it lets MDE report each device's **risk level** back to Intune so compliance can react to it.

## Onboarding through an Intune EDR policy

With the connector live, onboarding is a policy push. Go to **Endpoint security > Endpoint detection and response > Create policy** (platform Windows). Because the connector is on, Intune fills in the onboarding blob automatically; set *Sample sharing* and *Expedite telemetry reporting frequency* as desired, then assign to your device group. Confirm success two ways:

```powershell
# On an onboarded device, sense service should be running
Get-Service -Name Sense | Select-Object Name, Status, StartType

# Quick MDE protection state
Get-MpComputerStatus | Select-Object AMRunningMode, RealTimeProtectionEnabled, IsTamperProtected
```

Within ~10-15 minutes the device appears under *Assets > Devices* in the Defender portal.

## Attack Surface Reduction: audit, tune, then block

ASR rules block the behaviors attackers rely on. The golden rule is **never deploy straight to block** — start in **Audit**, watch what *would* have been blocked, add exclusions, then enforce. Configure rules in Intune under *Endpoint security > Attack surface reduction > Create policy > Attack Surface Reduction Rules*. Real rules worth knowing:

- **Block credential stealing from lsass.exe** — `9e6c4e1f-7d60-472f-ba1a-a39ef669e4b2` (stops Mimikatz-style credential dumping).
- **Block all Office applications from creating child processes** — `d4f940ab-401b-4efc-aadc-ad5f3c50688a`.
- **Block executable content from email client and webmail** — `be9ba2d9-53ea-4cdc-84e5-9b1eeee46550`.
- **Block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands** — `d1e49aac-8f56-4280-b9ba-993a6d77406c`.
- **Block Win32 API calls from Office macros** — `92e97fa1-2edf-4476-bdd6-9dd0b4dddc7b`.
- **Use advanced protection against ransomware** — `c1db55ab-c21a-4637-bb3f-a12568109d35`.

Each rule's per-setting state is *Not configured / Audit / Block / Warn*. You can manage ASR audit/block centrally; on an endpoint you can confirm with PowerShell:

```powershell
# 1 = Block, 2 = Audit, 6 = Warn, 0 = Not configured
(Get-MpPreference).AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Ids
(Get-MpPreference).AttackSurfaceReductionRules_Actions
```

Review hits in the Defender portal's **attack surface reduction report**, add `AttackSurfaceReductionOnlyExclusions` for confirmed false positives, then flip to Block ring by ring.

## Controlled folder access and network protection

Two more proactive controls live in the same ASR policy family:

- **Controlled folder access** — anti-ransomware: only trusted apps may write to protected folders (Documents, Desktop, etc.). Roll it out in audit first too, because line-of-business apps often need to be explicitly allowed.
- **Network protection** — extends SmartScreen to all processes, blocking outbound connections to malicious domains/IPs and phishing sites. Also start in audit, then set to Block.

## Tamper protection and exposure score

**Tamper protection** locks Defender's own settings — real-time protection, cloud-delivered protection, and signature updates — so malware, scripts, or even local admins cannot switch them off. Enable it tenant-wide in the Defender portal (*Settings > Endpoints > Advanced features*) and/or via an Intune Antivirus/Security Experience policy.

Finally, **Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management** continuously assesses every onboarded device and produces an **exposure score** and a prioritized list of **security recommendations** (missing patches, weak configurations, risky software). A lower exposure score means a smaller attack surface; treat the top recommendations as your hardening backlog. Together, ASR plus a falling exposure score plus tamper protection give you a measurably harder fleet — and a reliable risk signal to feed the automated loop next.

slides.title: Defender for Endpoint: Onboarding & ASR
slides.narration: In this lesson we connect our devices to Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and switch on its proactive defenses. We will onboard through Intune, wire up the connector that shares device risk, and then roll out Attack Surface Reduction the safe way. The goal is a measurably harder fleet that also produces a trustworthy risk signal.

slides.title: MDE architecture
bullets: Cloud service + sensor already built into Windows
Telemetry streams to the Microsoft Defender portal
Onboard = register the sensor with your tenant
No separate agent to install on modern Windows
slides.narration: Defender for Endpoint is a cloud brain paired with a sensor that ships inside Windows. You do not install a heavy agent; you onboard the device so its sensor reports to your tenant. Everything you investigate lives in the Microsoft Defender portal.

slides.title: The Intune <-> MDE connector
bullets: Defender portal: Advanced features > Intune connection On
Intune: Endpoint security > MDE connector Available
Connect Windows devices = On
Lets MDE report device risk back to Intune
slides.narration: Before anything else, wire the two services together. Turn on the Intune connection in the Defender portal and confirm it shows Available in Intune. This trust is what lets MDE feed each device's risk level back to Intune, which we will exploit heavily in the next lesson.

slides.title: Onboard via EDR policy
bullets: Endpoint security > EDR > Create policy (Windows)
Onboarding blob auto-filled by the connector
Assign to device group
Verify the Sense service is running
slides.code:
Get-Service -Name Sense |
  Select Name, Status, StartType
Get-MpComputerStatus |
  Select RealTimeProtectionEnabled, IsTamperProtected
slides.narration: With the connector live, onboarding is just a policy push. Intune fills in the onboarding details automatically, you assign it to a group, and within minutes the devices show up in the portal. On the endpoint, the Sense service running confirms the sensor is active.

slides.title: ASR: audit then block
bullets: Never deploy straight to Block
Audit logs what would be blocked
Add exclusions for real business apps
Flip to Block ring by ring
slides.narration: Attack Surface Reduction rules are powerful but can break legitimate apps. The discipline is always the same: audit first, study what would have been blocked, exclude the false positives, then enforce block mode gradually across deployment rings.

slides.title: Real ASR rules to know
bullets: Block credential stealing from lsass.exe
Block Office apps creating child processes
Block executable content from email/webmail
Block PsExec/WMI process creation; anti-ransomware
slides.code:
# lsass theft : 9e6c4e1f-7d60-472f-ba1a-a39ef669e4b2
# Office child: d4f940ab-401b-4efc-aadc-ad5f3c50688a
# email exec  : be9ba2d9-53ea-4cdc-84e5-9b1eeee46550
# PsExec/WMI  : d1e49aac-8f56-4280-b9ba-993a6d77406c
slides.narration: Learn a handful of these by name. Blocking credential theft from LSASS shuts down Mimikatz; blocking Office child processes stops the classic macro-spawns-PowerShell chain. Knowing the GUIDs lets you script and report on them precisely.

slides.title: Folder access, network, tamper
bullets: Controlled folder access: anti-ransomware write protection
Network protection: block malicious domains/IPs
Tamper protection: lock Defender settings
Audit-first for folder access and network too
slides.narration: Controlled folder access stops ransomware from mass-encrypting your documents, and network protection blocks connections to malicious sites. Tamper protection is the safety lock: it stops malware or even local admins from turning Defender off.

slides.title: Exposure score & recap
bullets: Defender Vulnerability Management scores every device
Exposure score = size of your attack surface
Security recommendations = your hardening backlog
Harder fleet + reliable risk signal for Lesson 3
slides.narration: Defender Vulnerability Management continuously grades your fleet and hands you a prioritized list of fixes. Drive the exposure score down by working the top recommendations. With ASR enforced and risk signals flowing, we are ready to automate device isolation next.
